name: SSO Authentication
description: OIDC/OAuth2 single sign-on with group-based library access.
overview: Single sign-on for Jellyfin against any OIDC provider, with users and library permissions driven by IdP groups.

versions.changelog:
## Changes

- An ID token that carries no `iat` claim is refused ([#216](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/216), [#221](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/221))
- A key a provider published for encryption is no longer accepted as a signing key ([#220](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/220), [#221](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/221))
- A refusal message named an outcome that had not happened ([#217](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/217), [#221](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/221))
- New: *Signing algorithms* on the provider card pins what a provider may sign a token with, on the login and the back-channel logout path alike ([#219](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/219), [#222](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/222))
- The end-to-end suite waits for the web client and for the server's log instead of guessing how long either takes ([#224](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/224), [#225](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/225))
- The conformance harness attributes a refusal to whoever made it, and no longer pins an algorithm on the plan that must not have one ([#226](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/226))

**Nothing to do on upgrade.** *Signing algorithms* is empty by default, which is what every
release before this one did: all of the asymmetric algorithms accepted.

Every fix here came from the OpenID Foundation's conformance suite, run against the plugin
for the first time on 6 November — not a reader of the code but the other side of the
protocol, serving a provider that answers in one specific broken way and recording what
the client did with it. Both of its plans were then run again against the fixed plugin,
because a fix checked only by the tests written to close it has been checked by whoever
misread the specification in the first place: eight of eight on the logout side, and on
the login side the twenty-three modules that apply to this client.

The reasoning, the findings it did not raise, and the three faults the reruns found in the
harness rather than in the plugin: [the conformance run](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/blob/main/docs/reviews/2026-11-06-oidc-conformance.md).

**Update from 1.12.18 if you run it.** Twenty findings from two reviews in one day, and
three of them are things an operator notices rather than reads about.

## Fixes you will notice

- Quick Connect works again on a server with more than one provider — the picker built the
  ordinary login route and the code it carried was never read, so the browser signed in and
  the device waited for ever. Broken since 19 October ([#201](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/201), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- The plugin's configuration page loads on a server published under a sub-path, where it
  used to fetch its own API from the origin and get a 404 ([#199](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/199), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- A first login under a sub-path saves a server address the web client can use ([#202](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/202), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- Unlinking an account ends its sessions even when the first attempt fails, and can be
  retried; before, the link was gone and nothing could reach those sessions again ([#203](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/203), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- A back-channel logout signed with a key the provider has just rotated to is accepted
  instead of refused for the rest of the cache's half hour ([#200](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/200), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- A profile-picture fetch has one deadline over the whole fetch, so a host that answers
  with headers and then silence no longer holds a login open ([#205](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/205), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- A group mapping naming something that is not a library id no longer turns every login
  into a 500 ([#193](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/193), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- A username the provider sends with a leading space no longer creates a second account
  that reads like the first ([#190](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/190), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))

## Harder to get wrong

- An ID token issued for another application is refused when its audience happens to name
  this one as well — `azp` is checked now ([#184](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/184), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- Signature algorithms are pinned to the asymmetric ones, so a symmetric key in a
  provider's public JWKS cannot decide whether a token is genuine ([#185](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/185), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- The userinfo answer has to be about the person who logged in, as OIDC Core requires —
  what is read there decides groups, libraries and the administrator flag ([#186](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/186), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- A discovery document cannot move the end-session endpoint to another host, which is where
  a logout sends the user's own ID token ([#187](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/187), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- The back channel no longer follows redirects, so a 307 cannot move a token request after
  its address has been checked ([#191](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/191), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- A name or group from a token cannot forge a line in the server log ([#189](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/189), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- An unreadable client-secret file is reported without naming the path to an anonymous
  caller ([#192](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/192), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- An implausible `iat` in a logout token is refused as a token rather than answered with a
  500 ([#195](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/195), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))
- The logout endpoint is behind the request limiter like every other anonymous one ([#194](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/194), [#196](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/196))

## Promises that only held while nothing happened at once

- Two administrators signing in at the same moment can no longer both be demoted. Each saw
  the other as the one who would be left, which locks everybody out of the server ([#198](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/198), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))
- Two self-service link callbacks finishing together can no longer write two links for one
  account, or two accounts for one identity ([#204](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/204), [#207](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/207))

## Also

- A guide for [Tinyauth](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/blob/main/docs/tinyauth.md)
  as a fourth provider, written against a login walked by hand, with what it costs — its
  local accounts have no groups ([#181](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/181))
- `SsoController` was a thousand lines and is now six files, none over 450 ([#182](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/issues/182), [#183](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/pull/183))

## Why this release is too long

Sixteen lines does not fit on a phone, and this repository's own rule says that means the
release is too large rather than the notes. It is. Two reviews landed on one afternoon: a
hardening pass over the whole plugin, and then the first review by something that did not
write it — eight findings, all eight real, three of them in code written that same morning.
Splitting them into two releases would have meant leaving the first eight open overnight.

The reasoning behind each is in the reviews rather than here:
[the hardening pass](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/blob/main/docs/reviews/2026-11-05-hardening.md),
[the outside review](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/blob/main/docs/reviews/2026-11-05-outside-review.md),
[the test practices audit](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/blob/main/docs/reviews/2026-11-05-test-practices.md).

565 unit tests, 131 end-to-end, 16 real-provider logins against Authentik, Keycloak and
Authelia, mutation score 70.29 %.

**Update from 1.12.17.** Two of that release's security fixes did not hold, and one of
them left the administrator escalation it claimed to close still open.

1.12.17 was the result of a review of the whole plugin. This release is the result of
reviewing *that* — thirteen changes written by one model and read by nobody else — along
with the surfaces nobody had audited at all: the release pipeline, the administrator's
browser, what happens under load, and the test suite itself.

## Why this one matters if you run 1.12.17

**The browser cookie was read under either name.** 1.12.17 gave the pending-login and
logout cookies the `__Host-` prefix, which a browser accepts only from a secure origin,
with no domain attribute, at the root path — so a neighbour on a sibling subdomain cannot
set it. Then it read the cookie under the prefixed name *or* the bare one, and the bare
name is exactly what that neighbour can set. The fallback applied whenever no prefixed
cookie was there, which is the normal state.

That gave back the escalation from 1.12.17's headline fix: plant a pending-login cookie
carrying your own browser id, start a login, hold the `state`, and have somebody else's
browser finish it. One name is read now, the one the deployment sets.

In the same release, the logout refused `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` — and a page on a
sibling subdomain sends `same-site`, which passed. The two halves of that commit disagreed
about who the attacker was.

**The logo fetch waived the address rules it was given.** The same release confined
outbound fetches by address and then passed `allowPrivateNetworks: true` on the logo path.
That flag returns "allowed" *before* anything is resolved, so the rules applied to no
redirect hop at all — on the one path whose answer comes back out through an endpoint
anybody can load, cached for twelve hours, with provider logos on by default. Its own test
took the default and so proved a property the shipping caller had opted out of.

## The rest

- **Pressing Save in the dashboard could resurrect a deleted link**, and no race was
  needed: the page posts the configuration it loaded with, and that body carried the
  links. Remove a link on the Links tab, save a provider, and the identity it belonged to
  signs into that account again. The mirror case erased a link made while the page was
  open, and that person's next login was refused as a username collision.
- **The back-channel logout spent a token before the sessions were gone.** A failure in
  between turned the provider's retry into a refused replay, and the sessions it had ended
  lived on.
- **A key rotation stopped every login for half an hour**, as a 500 rather than a refusal.
  An unknown key now refetches the provider's keys once.
- **A flood of logins could evict a chosen person's**, at a chosen moment, in a way that
  looks to them like their own mistake. The store keeps what it has and refuses what is
  new.
- **A pull request could decide whether it was tested.** The four required checks ran a
  filter script from the branch under test; a pull request that made it answer `code=false`
  passed all four with nothing executed. The base commit's copy decides now.
- Two workflows spliced text somebody else chose into a shell. The release ZIP was built
  from `main` while its provenance attestation named the tag. Nothing checked that the
  manifest's URLs point at this repository or that its checksums match the files.
- The address rules were weaker than they read: IPv6 barely checked, the provider
  exemption ignoring the port, and a name that could resolve differently between the check
  and the connection.

## What changed in how this is tested

Several of the above were invisible to the suite by construction, so the suite changed too.

The test provider now refuses what a real one refuses — an unregistered redirect at
authorize time, an unregistered post-logout redirect at the end-session endpoint. That one
gap is why a post-logout URL carrying the sub-path twice passed the test that asserted it.
A login behind a sub-path is now a test, with the harness standing in for the proxy.

The ID-token path can be handed a claim in the wrong shape, which it never could: the
generator only emitted strings, while the userinfo path has been tested against arrays,
objects and numbers for a long time. That asymmetry is where 1.12.17's blank-subject bug
came from, and the new generator found another on its first run — a `preferred_username`
that is a JSON object became a Jellyfin account called `{"given":"ben"}`.

Three tests were rewritten rather than added to, including the one sink where reverting a
1.12.17 fix left all 469 tests green. And the mutation score now says what it covers:
eight of the thirteen defects in the first review lived in the half it does not measure.

## Numbers

498 unit tests and 121 end-to-end tests on every push, against Jellyfin 12.0, 12.1 and
12.2, plus 16 logins through the real forms of Authentik, Keycloak and Authelia. Several of
the new cases fail against 1.12.17 on purpose, which I checked by putting the old code
back rather than assuming.

Full list: issues #153 to #168.

A security release. A review of the whole plugin — not of a diff — found thirteen
defects, and all thirteen are fixed and covered by tests that run the attack rather than
the defence.

## Read this first if you already run this

Four things behave differently. None of them needs action on an ordinary setup.

- **`DELETE /sso/link/self` now requires `?providerId=…`** and ends that account's
  sessions. Without a provider named it used to remove *every* link the caller had.
  Nothing in the interface calls this endpoint, so this matters only to a script.
- **A profile picture is no longer fetched from a private address.** The provider's own
  host and any public address were always fine; loopback, RFC 1918, link-local and
  container names are now refused. *Allow profile pictures from this network*, new on the
  configuration page, lifts that for a household that serves avatars from a second
  machine.
- **A discovery document must name `jwks_uri`, `token_endpoint` and `userinfo_endpoint`
  on the authority's own host.** Verified against Authentik, Keycloak and Authelia; the
  browser-facing endpoints are deliberately not checked, because a provider may be
  reachable under one name from the server and another from the browser. A provider that
  splits the server-facing ones across hosts would now be refused.
- **A `ConfidentialSecretRef` without an `env:` or `file:` prefix is refused when
  saving.** If you pasted a literal client secret into that field, move it to
  `env:VARIABLE` or `file:/path` — and **rotate it**, because it was readable by anyone
  who could trigger a callback. See below.

## The one that mattered

**Any account holder could make themselves an administrator.** A pending login was not
tied to the browser that began it: the `state` travels through the identity provider and
back, so holding one proved nothing about who started the flow. The self-service link
endpoint handed out a genuine provider URL carrying the caller's own user id. Sent to
somebody in an administrator-mapped group — and completing silently if they had a live
provider session — it attached that person's subject to the attacker's account. The
victim's next login then wrote the victim's groups onto it, administrator flag included,
and Jellyfin evaluates a policy per request, so a token issued long before became an
administrator token. The victim also landed in the attacker's account on every later
login.

A cookie now binds the flow: minted when the login starts, required when the callback
arrives, and a state presented by the wrong browser is refused *and spent*. The same gap
let a login be completed in a stranger's browser, which is fixed by the same cookie.

## The rest

**The client secret was readable by anonymous callers.** The callback returned exception
text verbatim, and one of those messages quoted the configured secret reference — a field
nothing validated, with no control on the page, that the documentation told you to edit by
hand. Two anonymous requests were enough. The message no longer quotes the value, the
callback no longer hands out exception text, and the admin API refuses a reference that is
not `env:` or `file:`.

**Two server-side request forgeries, both with the response coming back out.** A
provider's branding document could name an absolute URL for its logo, which left the
provider's host entirely — and the endpoint that serves the result is anonymous, so
anything on the container network answering with an image came back to an unauthenticated
caller and was cached for twelve hours. A profile picture URL, which on several providers
is a user-editable attribute, had no address check at all. Redirects were followed by the
HTTP handler, so nothing looked at the second address in a chain; they are now followed by
hand, three hops, every hop checked.

**A logout that aborted.** On a server published under a sub-path, the post-logout
redirect carried the prefix twice, so providers refused it as unregistered and left the
user on an error page with their provider session alive. Every existing test ran at the
root, where the two forms are identical.

**A self-unlink made tokens unrevocable.** Back-channel logout finds an account through
its link and nothing else, so removing your own link opted your sessions out of
provider-driven revocation — the operator could disable you at the provider while the
plugin revoked "0 account(s)" and your tokens kept working. Unlinking ends them now.

**Smaller, and real.** A blank `sub` was accepted, so every user whose provider mapped an
empty attribute landed in the *first* such person's account. A logout token could be
replayed for the five minutes its `iat` stayed fresh. A policy that could not be read was
replaced with a blank one, which could silently re-enable a disabled account. An
apostrophe was allowed in a forwarded path and spliced into JavaScript string literals. A
JSON escaper was supplying an HTML attribute and an HTML escaper a CSS selector. The pages
carrying a one-time secret were cacheable unless an unrelated switch happened to be on,
the approval page could be framed and its click stolen, and the logout could be triggered
from any site.

**Eleven documentation claims did not hold** and are corrected. The threat model now
carries both directions of the linking attack, says plainly that it was written by the
same model that wrote the code and that a review found thirteen things it had not
accounted for, and admits that the forwarded headers are read from whoever sends the
request.

## Numbers

469 unit tests and 112 end-to-end tests on every push, against Jellyfin 12.0, 12.1 and
12.2, plus 16 logins through the real forms of Authentik, Keycloak and Authelia. The
suite grew by 74 unit and 14 end-to-end cases in this release, and several of them fail
against the old code on purpose — I checked by putting it back.

Full list: issues #126 to #138.

## What is new

- **Refuse a login that matches no group mapping.** Off by default. With it on, somebody
  in no mapped group is turned away instead of getting an account with no libraries —
  a second lock inside the plugin for the day the provider is the thing configured
  wrongly. It applies to accounts that already exist: once the **last** mapped group is
  gone, so is the login — losing one of several only changes what the account can see.
  Users excluded from the group sync stay exempt, and local passwords are untouched, so a
  mistyped claim name cannot lock you out of your own server.
- **Single logout now tells the provider which session is ending.** The browser's last
  login keeps its ID token in server memory while *Sign out of the identity provider too*
  is on, and the logout sends it as `id_token_hint`, so a provider that used to ask the
  user to confirm ends the session instead. Nothing is kept while that setting is off.
- **The login button reaches the server from apps that run their own copy of the web
  client**, such as the Samsung one, when **Dashboard → Networking → Published server
  URIs** is set. Without it the button stays as it was.

## Before you upgrade

Nothing to do. The new refusal is off until you switch it on, and the logout hint only
applies where provider logout was already enabled.

If you use an app that packages its own web client and want the login button to work
there, set a published server URI. Which apps need that, and which sign in through Quick
Connect instead, is now written down: see [docs/clients.md](https://github.com/be-nj/jellyfin-sso/blob/main/docs/clients.md).
